sections.title: Part 2 · Instructional Clarity Framework Components
sections.instructions: Tap a component to expand it and rate the evidence observed.

studentActions: Students read and write in each class daily.
Students employ a variety of strategies — such as annotation, summarization, questioning, and using available resources — to comprehend and analyze complex texts.
Students support their ideas with textual evidence in discussions and writing, demonstrating critical thinking and deep engagement with the content.
teacherActions: Teachers intentionally provide opportunities for students to read and write daily.
Teachers provide strategies such as guided reading, text chunking, annotation techniques, and questioning to help students navigate, comprehend, and analyze challenging texts.
Teachers prompt students to cite textual evidence in discussions and writing, guiding them in analyzing and justifying their ideas through structured academic discourse.

studentActions: Students integrate academic vocabulary into their reading, writing, speaking, and listening, effectively articulating their thoughts and engaging in meaningful discussions.
teacherActions: Teachers use a variety of appropriately challenging and complex texts to intentionally model and reinforce the use of academic vocabulary across reading, writing, speaking, and listening, providing sentence stems, word banks, and discussion prompts to support student use.

Teachers engage students in how to learn new words and the meanings of specific words with intentional word selection, systematic and explicit direct instruction, morphology, and use of new words throughout language acquisition.

studentActions: Students understand the purpose and use the structures of the workshop model to monitor their progress toward meeting the success criteria.
Students participate in whole-group, small-group, and independent activities that allow them to produce evidence of learning.
Students use anchor charts, manipulatives, mentor texts, and graphic organizers to support learning and problem-solving.
teacherActions: Teachers explicitly communicate the purpose of the workshop model, establish clear routines, and support students in using structures (mini-lessons, work time, and share time) to monitor their progress toward meeting success criteria.

Teachers intentionally plan student work time for students to engage deeply with reading, writing, and problem-solving through mini-lessons, modeling, guided practice, and independent application across literacy and numeracy contexts.

Teachers integrate anchor charts, manipulatives, mentor texts, and graphic organizers into instruction, explicitly modeling how students can use these tools to support their learning and problem-solving.

studentActions: Students know the roles of all members of the team and hold themselves and each other accountable for learning.
Students engage in discourse, consider multiple perspectives, and empathetically respond to their peers to produce evidence of learning.
Students communicate their thinking through partner talk, small-group discussions, and whole-class reflections, using academic language and reasoning.
Students participate in two-way dialogues where students focus on a topic and explore it by building, challenging, and negotiating ideas.
teacherActions: Teachers explicitly define and reinforce team member roles, ensuring that students understand their responsibilities and hold themselves and each other accountable for contributing to the team’s learning.
Teachers model and reinforce the use of academic language and reasoning, guiding students in articulating their thinking through partner talk, small-group discussions, and whole-class reflections.

Teachers develop protocols and structure opportunities for students to engage in rich, student-led discussions where they build upon, challenge, and negotiate ideas to deepen understanding and produce evidence of learning.

studentActions: Students engage in a variety of formative assessment opportunities (e.g., discussions, written responses, problem-solving tasks, peer collaboration) to demonstrate their understanding and progress toward mastery in alignment with the summative assessment.
Students actively review and reflect on teacher feedback, using it to adjust their learning strategies, clarify misconceptions, and determine their next steps toward meeting the standard.
Students take ownership of their learning by tracking their progress, setting goals based on formative assessments, and making informed decisions about how to improve their mastery of concepts.
teacherActions: Teachers analyze summative assessments to plan instruction that provides multiple opportunities for students to demonstrate evidence of learning through diverse assessment methods, such as discussions, written reflections, problem-solving tasks, and performance-based activities.

Teachers create structures for students to analyze their progress, set learning goals, and determine next steps based on formative assessment results, fostering a sense of ownership in the learning process.
Teachers continuously analyze student responses and performance data to modify instruction, reteach concepts as needed, and provide targeted support to help all students progress toward mastery.

studentActions: Students use rubrics, success criteria, and exemplars to assess their own work and provide meaningful, standards-based feedback to peers.
Students actively revise and refine their work based on teacher and peer feedback, demonstrating a growth mindset and a commitment to improving their understanding.
Students use feedback to monitor their progress, make adjustments to their learning strategies, and set specific goals to achieve mastery of the learning target.
teacherActions: Teachers provide students with rubrics, exemplars, and clear success criteria to guide self-reflection, peer feedback, and understanding of expectations for mastery in alignment with the summative assessment.
Teachers give specific, targeted, and constructive feedback that is directly tied to learning goals, ensuring students understand what steps to take for improvement.
Teachers create structured opportunities for students to immediately apply feedback by revising their work, discussing next steps, and refining their understanding.

studentActions: Students contribute their unique backgrounds, experiences, and viewpoints to classroom discussions while actively listening to and valuing the perspectives of their peers.
Students participate in discussions that highlight diverse voices, cultures, and lived experiences, recognizing the importance of their individual contributions to the learning community.
Students make meaningful connections between academic content and their own cultural and linguistic backgrounds, applying their knowledge to real-world situations and experiences.
teacherActions: Teachers recognize, address and engage the students’ culture, linguistics, knowledge and skills to ensure that they are embedded in their daily practice.
Teachers thoughtfully choose texts, resources, and learning tasks that reflect and affirm the diverse backgrounds of students, ensuring that all voices and perspectives are represented.
Teachers embed explicit language acquisition instruction through the use of the 4 language domains in all lessons (and all content areas) for all students.

Teachers employ targeted scaffolding techniques — such as visuals, sentence frames, small-group support, and differentiated instruction — to ensure that all students, including multilingual learners and those receiving special education services, can engage meaningfully with grade-level content.

responseOptions.label: No
responseOptions.definition: There’s no target visible or communicated during the visit, or what’s posted isn’t derived from the content-area standard at all — it’s a task description, activity name, or something unrelated.

responseOptions.label: Partial
responseOptions.definition: A target is posted, but it isn’t pulled directly from the standard — it paraphrases, narrows, or drifts from the standard’s actual language or intent.

responseOptions.label: Yes
responseOptions.definition: The target is taken directly from the content-area standard — its language and intent match what the standard calls for.

responseOptions.label: No Learning Target
responseOptions.definition: A target was expected to be visible by this point but wasn’t provided at all. This is a real finding, not a timing gap — it stays in scoring.

responseOptions.label: Retrieval
responseOptions.definition: Recalling facts or carrying out a known procedure.

responseOptions.label: Comprehension
responseOptions.definition: Explaining or representing the key ideas within a concept.

responseOptions.label: Analysis
responseOptions.definition: Breaking down knowledge to draw new conclusions or make comparisons.

responseOptions.label: Knowledge Utilization
responseOptions.definition: Using knowledge purposefully in a real task — building an argument, testing an idea, or applying it across more than one standard.

responseOptions.label: No Evidence
responseOptions.definition: Students had a chance to produce evidence by this point but didn’t, or the visit ran long enough that evidence should exist and doesn’t.

responseOptions.label: Retrieval
responseOptions.definition: Recalling facts or carrying out a known procedure — based on what students actually said, wrote, made, or did.

responseOptions.label: Comprehension
responseOptions.definition: Explaining or representing the key ideas within a concept — based on what students actually said, wrote, made, or did.

responseOptions.label: Analysis
responseOptions.definition: Breaking down knowledge to draw new conclusions or make comparisons — based on what students actually said, wrote, made, or did.

responseOptions.label: Knowledge Utilization
responseOptions.definition: Using knowledge purposefully in a real task — based on what students actually said, wrote, made, or did.

responseOptions.label: BEHIND pacing
responseOptions.definition: A week and a half or more behind where the pacing guide indicates the class should be.

responseOptions.label: ON pace
responseOptions.definition: Within 5 days on either side of where the pacing guide indicates the class should be.

responseOptions.label: AHEAD of pacing
responseOptions.definition: More than a week and a half ahead of where the pacing guide indicates the class should be.
The learning has no clear connection to the adopted curriculum or to grade/course-level expectations — materials and content appear to come from elsewhere.
A loose connection to the adopted curriculum is visible, but the content sits noticeably below or outside grade/course-level expectations.
The learning is generally grounded in the adopted curriculum at grade/course level, though the connection is uneven or partly implicit.
The learning is clearly grounded in the adopted curriculum and matches grade/course-level expectations throughout the observed segment.
The learning is unmistakably grounded in the adopted curriculum at grade/course level, and students can name what they are learning and why it matters.
Intended curricular materials are absent, replaced, or used in ways that lose the rigor and purpose of the lesson.
Some intended materials are present, but they are used superficially or in ways that noticeably reduce the intended rigor.
Students use the intended materials, though not always as designed — some of the intended rigor or purpose is diluted.
Students use the intended high-quality materials largely as designed, preserving the rigor and purpose of the lesson.
Students use the intended materials, tools, technology, and manipulatives fully as designed, and the rigor and purpose of the lesson are preserved throughout.
There is no evidence students know what they are learning or what success looks like — no target or success criteria are communicated.
A target is posted or stated, but students show little sign of understanding it, and success criteria are absent or unclear.
Students have some sense of what they are learning; success criteria exist but are used inconsistently or only by the teacher.
Students can generally explain what they are learning, and success criteria are communicated clearly and referenced during the lesson.
Students can articulate what they are learning and what high-quality work looks like, and actively use the success criteria to judge their own progress.
Tasks do not connect to the target/standard, or they require thinking well below what the standard calls for.
Tasks connect to the target’s content but sit at a noticeably lower level of thinking or produce little usable evidence of learning.
Tasks partially match the target’s intent — some require the called-for thinking, others fall short or stop at recall.
Tasks require the level of thinking and rigor the target/standard calls for, and students produce evidence aligned to that intent.
Tasks consistently require the full thinking, rigor, and evidence called for by the target/standard, and student work demonstrates it.
The teacher delivers the meaning of the text/content; students receive it without being asked to make meaning themselves.
Students are occasionally asked a recall question, but the teacher still does nearly all of the meaning-making.
Students do some meaning-making — answering text-based questions or annotating — but the teacher still supplies most conclusions.
Students regularly make meaning from the text/content by citing evidence, questioning, analyzing, or explaining their thinking.
Students consistently do the meaning-making — citing evidence, questioning, analyzing, and explaining — and the teacher’s role is to prompt and press, not to supply the answer.
No reading, writing, speaking, or listening with text/content is taking place, or the material is far below grade level.
Some engagement with text/content occurs, but it is brief, passive, or noticeably below grade-level complexity.
Students engage with grade-level text/content, though participation is uneven or the work stays at the easier end of the range.
Students are actively reading, writing, speaking, and/or listening with appropriately challenging grade-level text or content.
All students are actively engaged with appropriately complex grade-level text or content across multiple modes — reading, writing, speaking, and listening.
No academic or discipline-specific vocabulary is taught or reinforced during the lesson.
Vocabulary appears incidentally — a word is mentioned or defined in passing, with no intentional instruction.
Some vocabulary is taught intentionally, but selection seems incidental or the words are not reinforced within the context of the learning.
Essential academic and discipline-specific words are intentionally selected, explicitly taught, and reinforced within the lesson’s context.
Intentionally selected essential vocabulary is explicitly taught through systematic instruction (including word parts/morphology) and reinforced repeatedly throughout the learning.
Students are not expected to use academic vocabulary; it is not present in their speaking or writing.
Students may repeat a word back, but there is no expectation that they use it in their own reasoning or work.
Students use some academic vocabulary when prompted, though accuracy is inconsistent or use is limited to a few students.
Students are expected to and do use newly learned academic vocabulary accurately in speaking, writing, reasoning, or discussion.
Students consistently and accurately use newly learned academic vocabulary across modes — speaking, writing, reasoning, and discussion — with supports such as stems or word banks used as needed.
There is no discernible structure — instruction does not move from modeling toward student application.
Some explicit teaching occurs, but students never move into guided or independent application within the lesson.
The lesson includes modeling and application, but the release toward independence is abrupt, uneven, or incomplete.
Instruction is structured so students move from explicit teaching/modeling into guided and then increasingly independent application.
The release of responsibility is deliberate and visible — students move purposefully from modeling to guided to independent application, and use the structure to monitor their own progress.
The teacher does nearly all of the cognitive work; students primarily watch and listen.
Students do some work, but the large majority of thinking and talking is still done by the teacher.
The cognitive work is split — students do a meaningful share, but teacher-led delivery still takes up much of the time.
Students do the majority of the cognitive work through reading, writing, discussing, reasoning, problem-solving, or applying.
Students are clearly doing the cognitive heavy lifting throughout, producing evidence of learning, while the teacher facilitates and monitors.
There is no student-to-student academic dialogue; any talk is off-topic or teacher-directed only.
Students talk briefly, but the exchange is procedural (“what page?”) rather than academic reasoning.
Students explain their thinking to peers, but the dialogue is mostly one-way — little responding, questioning, or building on ideas.
Students engage in purposeful academic dialogue — explaining thinking, responding to others, and asking questions.
Students sustain rich, student-led dialogue in which they explain, question, build upon, challenge, and negotiate ideas using academic language.
Students are grouped but there is no structure requiring contribution; some students do nothing.
Students work near each other rather than with each other — no roles, and one or two students carry the work.
Some structure exists (roles or a protocol), but accountability is inconsistent and participation is uneven.
The structure requires individual accountability, and most students contribute meaningfully to the team’s learning.
Roles and protocols are clear and reinforced; every student is individually accountable and contributes meaningfully to the team’s evidence of learning.
No evidence of learning is elicited; the teacher proceeds without checking understanding.
The teacher checks in with a few volunteers or asks “any questions?”, which surfaces little real evidence.
The teacher elicits evidence from some students, but not broadly enough to know who understands and who does not.
The teacher actively elicits evidence of learning from multiple students across the class during the lesson.
The teacher systematically elicits evidence from all students through varied methods, building a clear picture of who understands, who does not, and why.
Information gathered is not used; instruction proceeds unchanged regardless of student understanding.
A brief acknowledgment of confusion occurs, but no real adjustment to instruction or next steps follows.
Some adjustment occurs — a reteach or a hint — but it is limited or does not reach the students who need it.
The teacher and/or students use the evidence to adjust instruction, strategy, grouping, pacing, or next steps.
Evidence drives visible, responsive change — instruction, grouping, or pacing shifts in the moment, and students use it to set goals and determine their own next steps.
No feedback is given, or feedback is limited to marks and general praise with no connection to the learning target.
Feedback is evaluative rather than instructional (“good job,” “not quite”) and does not point to next steps.
Some feedback is specific, but it is inconsistent across students or only loosely tied to the success criteria.
Students receive specific feedback tied to the learning target/success criteria that clarifies where they are and what to do next.
Feedback is consistently specific, targeted, and tied to success criteria — from the teacher and from peers using rubrics and exemplars — and clearly names next steps.
Students do not act on feedback; there is no opportunity to revise during the lesson.
Students receive feedback but move on without using it; any revision is limited to fixing a marked answer.
Some students act on feedback when directed, but revision is not a routine part of the learning.
Students use feedback to revise, refine, or improve their work or thinking during the learning process.
Students routinely and independently apply feedback to revise and refine their work, monitor progress, and set goals toward mastery.
Students’ cultural and linguistic backgrounds are absent from the materials, tasks, and discussion.
Representation is superficial or decorative — present on a wall, but not part of the learning.
Some texts, resources, or discussion reflect students’ backgrounds, but the connection is occasional rather than intentional.
Texts, resources, and tasks intentionally reflect and affirm students’ diverse backgrounds, and students contribute their perspectives.
Students’ cultures, languages, and experiences are woven throughout the learning — students draw on them to make meaning and connect content to real-world experience.
No scaffolds or language supports are present; some students cannot access the grade-level content.
Minimal supports exist, or support is provided by lowering the demand rather than scaffolding access to grade-level work.
Some scaffolds are in place, but they are inconsistent or do not reach all students who need them.
Targeted scaffolds and language supports allow all students, including multilingual learners and students with disabilities, to engage with grade-level content.
Explicit language instruction across the four domains and well-matched scaffolds are embedded throughout, and every student engages meaningfully with grade-level content.
Adults rarely initiate interaction with students; exchanges are impersonal, transactional, or negative.
A few adults greet or acknowledge students, but positive personal interaction is inconsistent and names are seldom used.
Adults generally interact positively with students, though warmth and personal interest vary by adult or by student.
Adults consistently greet students by name, check in, listen, and show interest in them as individuals.
Every adult observed initiates warm, personal interaction — using names, greeting, checking in, listening closely — and students are visibly known as individuals.
Students avoid adults or do not seek help; requests that are made are ignored or dismissed.
Only a few students approach adults, and responses are inconsistent, rushed, or perfunctory.
Students approach adults when needed, and adults generally respond supportively, though attentiveness varies.
Students readily approach and seek assistance from adults, and adults respond with attention, respect, and support.
Students seek out adults comfortably and often, and adults consistently respond with full attention, respect, and meaningful support.
Peer interactions are exclusionary, disrespectful, or negative; students do not listen to or support one another.
Some positive peer interaction occurs, but exclusion, side conversations, or dismissiveness are also evident.
Students generally interact respectfully, though inclusion and encouragement are uneven across groups or spaces.
Students consistently listen to, include, help, and encourage one another across classrooms and common spaces.
Inclusive, respectful peer relationships are the clear norm — students actively listen, include, help, and encourage each other without adult prompting.
Expectations are unclear or absent, and adult responses to behavior are inconsistent, harsh, or undermine student dignity.
Expectations exist but are unevenly communicated or enforced; adult responses are sometimes reactive or publicly corrective.
Expectations and routines are generally clear and reinforced, and most adult responses are calm and respectful.
Expectations and routines are clearly communicated and consistently reinforced, and adults respond calmly and respectfully.
Expectations and routines are clear, predictable, and consistently reinforced; adults respond to behavior calmly and privately in ways that fully preserve student dignity.
The experience is entirely adult-directed; students have no observable voice, choice, or responsibility.
Student voice is limited to token opportunities, or choice is confined to trivial matters.
Students have some opportunities for voice, choice, or responsibility, but these vary by setting and are adult-controlled.
Students regularly contribute ideas, make meaningful choices, and take on leadership or responsibility.
Students authentically shape their learning and school experience — contributing ideas, making meaningful choices, leading, and participating in decisions that affect them.
Disengaged or isolated students go unnoticed; adults do not approach or reconnect them.
Adults notice only the most visible cases, and responses tend to be corrective rather than reconnecting.
Adults notice and respond to many students who disengage, though some are missed or the follow-through is brief.
Adults notice when students disengage or struggle and consistently approach, support, redirect, and reconnect them.
Adults proactively monitor for disconnection and reliably reconnect students with warmth and support, so no student remains isolated or disengaged.
